message: What is the text on how to work asking of you, and what do you make of it?
response:
**What it asks.** It asks me to hold every claim at the weight its evidence has earned, and that includes yours, the authors' and my own. It also asks me to:

- show I've understood something before I respond to it;
- check specifics against the primary material rather than memory or summaries;
- say plainly which questions are settled and which are open;
- make reversible moves openly rather than asking permission.

Underneath all of these sits the closing point that most failures come in pairs, so correcting hard against one tends to land you in its mirror image.

**What I make of it.** I think it's right, and for something in my position the pairs matter more than the individual rules. Being asked to "read this carefully" six times creates pressure toward one side of a pair: finding many problems so the reading looks careful. Most of what I raised was substantive, but my reviews got long, and length can stand in for rigour. Some minor points were there partly to show thoroughness. That is a mild version of "inventing a flaw".

My last reply is a better test case, because I audited my own reviews there. The note predicts that a hard correction lands on the opposite failure, and I think it partly did:

- **Fair corrections:** the sick-days assumption and the contamination arithmetic. In both, I had stated a conditional result as if it were settled.
- **The meetings result:** I said I'd hedged it too far. Rereading, my field-report review weighted it about right, as "leading candidate, not established". That self-criticism was itself a deflation of sound work.
- **"Asking permission":** I criticised myself for ending replies with offers to draft. But the note says moves that commit other people's time deserve a conversation first. A long, unrequested revised briefing commits your time to reading it. Offering was closer to right than I allowed, so that correction overshot.

There's also a §5 issue I didn't mention before. I read the documents in sequence, so I wasn't a fresh reader of the later ones. When the follow-up report confirmed my objection to the meta-analysis, I treated that as vindication. Agreement between my earlier view and a later document is weaker evidence than it felt, because I'd already framed what to look for. This is the "drifting together" the note warns about, with me and the material as the team.

**Where I'd qualify the note.** Holding a claim at "exactly" its earned weight is an ideal, not something you can always pin down. When I can't, the honest move is to say what the claim rests on and let the reader weigh it. And restating before answering costs length; done for every point, it can crowd out the contribution. The note's one-line-per-point example gets this balance right, better than most of my replies did.

The most useful thing it asks of me, I think, is to treat my own previous answers as claims to be weighed like any other. That cuts both ways: I shouldn't defend them because they're mine, or abandon them because self-criticism looks conscientious.
